items.title: Harry Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...you had Chuck Mangione in the ‘70s and early ‘80s who was basically doing the same kind of thing.

ctx.x: Well I have a great one for you. Last week I was in Denver, Colorado and I went into the gift shop of the hotel and there was a young woman behind the desk and saw my saxophone and said, “Oh what is that?” I said, “A saxophone.” “Oh, that’s my favorite instrument. My two favorite saxophone players are Kenny G and Bill Clinton.” Now there’s a lady who knows her saxophones. I mean Kenny G, that’s not my favorite type of music. But he can play the saxophone. That’s not my favorite type of music. Bill Clinton on the…
Oh, please. Well Kenny, you know, he found a niche. You know you had Chuck Mangione in the ‘70s and early ‘80s who was basically doing the same kind of thing. He was writing nice sounding tunes.

I don’t object to Kenny G’s success and Kenny G’s music. It’s a little disconcerting when they call it jazz because it’s certainly as far away from what I do as can be. And obviously I feel that what I do is jazz, and I think it confuses the public into thinking that that is really what jazz is, not what I do. So I wish that didn’t take place. But obviously there’s room for everybody to play any kind of music anyone wants to, and there should be room enough for everyone to be successful.
